metadata.title: Where the Record Stops
metadata.subject_line: How to build from a company's disclosure without inventing authority

beats.narration_text: You want to build something from what a company published. So you read everything they put out. And about ten minutes in, you hit the first thing they didn't say. That right there is the actual job. Not the building. What you do at the gap.

props.command: Build it from what they actually said.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Tanmay Kulkarni, in for Humanitarians AI. I build reference implementations — working code that ships next to a case study, so you can see how a system behaves instead of reading a diagram of it. This one's a credit-memo tool at DBS Bank. And before anything else, the thing I want to be really clear about: this is not DBS's system. It's mine. I built it from what DBS published, and everywhere the public record stopped, I either labelled what I'd invented or left it deliberately empty. That's what I want to talk about — how you do that honestly.

artifactLines: It does not replicate DBS's agent architecture, agent count, or task breakdown.
It does not replicate their data sources or review process.
It should not be cited as evidence of DBS's technical design.
Built from what DBS publicly confirmed — plus labelled construction everywhere the record stops.

beats.narration_text: Every single thing in a build like this is one of three. Confirmed — the company actually said it. Constructed — I invented it, because code has to run and they didn't say. Or blank — I left it empty on purpose, and made it impossible to skip past. I label all three, out loud, in the code. And then there's one rule I try not to break: never put a construction where a judgement goes.

beats.narration_text: So what did DBS actually say? Specialised agents handling more than seventy tasks — tasks, not agents, and that's their word. Raw data goes in, a review-ready first draft comes out. About fifteen hundred people using it. And a target: cut memo prep by at least thirty percent, on work that can eat up to forty percent of a relationship manager's week. That's the confirmed set for the tool itself. Everything else, I built.

beats.narration_text: There's one more thing DBS said, and it isn't about the tool at all — it's about how they're governing all of this. Their own data chief, on the record: capability is moving at five, governance and control are moving at one, and they're not allowing autonomy until that closes. A bank saying that out loud is unusual, and it's to their credit. It's also a design instruction, if you're listening.

props.quote: …there's a gap and we need to close this gap before we allow autonomy.
props.attribution: Nimish Panchmatia, Chief Data and Transformation Officer, DBS — Computer Weekly, 28 July 2026
props.sparkLine: They said it first, and on the record.

beats.narration_text: Now the parts I made up. How a memo request arrives — DBS never said, so I defined three fields and wrote down that I'd defined them. Looking up a client record. Noticing when data is missing. The final hand-off, which in mine is a stub that does nothing, because DBS's real credit-approval process isn't something they've described. All invented. All labelled, in the file, where the next person will actually see it.

beats.narration_text: And then there's the one I left empty. Somewhere in this pipeline a human decides whether a draft is good enough to go forward. I could have invented that. A confidence score. A dollar threshold. It would have looked finished — and it would have shipped a policy nobody chose, to whoever picked this up next. So the gate has nothing in it. No score, no threshold, no rule. It won't even start unless you hand it a real decision function. Where the record stopped, I stopped.

props.title: src/human_review_gate.py
props.code:
# deliberately absent by design,
# not a gap to fill.

# No confidence score, no dollar
# threshold, no severity rule is
# invented here.

def __init__(self, decision_function: …):
    if … not callable(decision_function):
        raise TypeError(
            "HumanReviewGate requires a "
            "callable decision_function …"
        )
props.sparkLine: Where the record stopped, I stopped.

beats.narration_text: There's one more line, and it's the one I'd defend hardest. If the decision function hands back something the gate doesn't recognise — a typo, a wrong string, anything — it raises. It does not continue. Because a gate that shrugs and carries on when it's confused isn't a gate. That's called failing open, and it's how systems end up approving things nobody approved. Mine fails closed. On purpose.

props.title: src/human_review_gate.py
props.code:
result = self._decision_function(draft)

if result not in VALID_OUTCOMES:
    raise ValueError(
        f"decision_function returned "
        f"{result!r}, which is not one of "
        f"the gate's recognized outcomes …"
        "The gate will not guess at what "
        "an unrecognized value should mean."
    )

return result
props.sparkLine: A gate that shrugs isn't a gate.

beats.narration_text: And that's not just a comment in the file. There's a test whose entire job is to prove it. It hands the gate a garbage answer, then checks that finalize was never called. Not that the result looked right — that the next step never ran at all. Sequencing, not output. Six modules, six test files, all passing.

props.title: tests/test_orchestrator.py
props.code:
# test_invalid_gate_return_value_
#     raises_instead_of_proceeding

with patch("orchestrator.finalize") as spy:
    try:
        orchestrator.run(
            request,
            decision_function=lambda d: "maybe"
        )
        assert False, "Expected ValueError"
    except ValueError:
        pass

    spy.assert_not_called()

beats.narration_text: Here's what building it actually changed. The plan had four stages. The code has five. Keeping draft synthesis a pure function — one that gets handed a client record instead of going and fetching one — meant client lookup needed its own stage, with its own stopping point. I didn't discover that by drawing it. I discovered it by running it. That's most of why I build these at all.

props.sparkLine: The plan had four. The code has five.
props.footnote: My decomposition, not DBS's. Discovered by running it, not by drawing it.

beats.narration_text: And here's the place the whole framework strains. My gate can reject a draft. But look at the workflow DBS's disclosure actually supports — the relationship manager reviews, edits, finalises, submits. One path. Nobody ever gets turned down. So which column does that rejection path go in? Neither, cleanly. The name came from their language. The path itself came from that governance quote — not from anything DBS walked through. So I called it a reasoned construction and wrote that down, rather than let it sit in the middle column looking solid.

beats.narration_text: So take whatever you're building. Go element by element and put each one in a column — confirmed, constructed, or deliberately blank. Most people have never done it, and they're surprised how much sits in the middle. Then find your gate and ask it three things. Does it start empty, or did you give it a default? What does it do with an answer it doesn't recognise? And has anyone ever actually seen it say no? If the answer to that last one is no, you've got a reasoned construction — same as me. Just label it.

props.title: Your turn
props.heading: Three questions for your gate
checks: Does it start empty, or did you give it a default?
What does it do with an answer it doesn't recognise?
Has anyone ever actually seen it say no?
props.sourceNote: Sort every element into one of them before you ship.

beats.narration_text: Where the record stops, the code stops. Everything after that is a decision you're making — so make it out loud. I'm Tanmay Kulkarni, for Humanitarians AI.
